extracted.intended_audience: political leaders, speechwriters, journalists, and students of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for creating persuasive public appeals and forming a common public will from diverse private opinions, drawn from analysis of political speeches, symbols, and mass communication. Useful for speechwriters, press-release authors, and political communicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple economic contacts affect opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's various economic contacts limit or enlarge the range of his opinions; but which contact produces a particular opinion is rarely obvious (e.g., landlord vs. employer vs. buyer). "Without special inquiry you cannot tell. The economic determinist cannot tell."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a single causal source for an individual's view; research and inquiry are needed to identify which social relations are shaping an opinion. Anti-pattern: attributing a stated opinion to a single economic role without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed set of opinions tied to social position
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no fixed set of opinions on any question that go with being the owner of a factory (or any other social position). Ownership predicts some tendencies (e.g., resisting deprivation of ownership) but cannot prophesy detailed policy views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid templates that assume uniform views for a social class; test messages rather than relying on deterministic stereotypes. Scoring note: messages that presuppose monolithic class views risk inaccuracy and backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interests and responses are learned and variable
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The craving and the action are both learned, and in another generation might be learned differently.’ Instincts and dispositions are shaped by experience and culture, so attachments change over time and across societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design communications assuming malleable attachments; education, conditioning, and framing can change responses. Anti-pattern: treating audience behavior as biologically fixed or permanently determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use binders/stereotypes (symbols) to transfer sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain words act as 'binders' or stereotypes (e.g., 'Lincoln') by which the piety or feeling surrounding the name can be transferred to the speaker or candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ well-known symbols or names to transfer favorable associations quickly across heterogeneous audiences. Example: invoking Lincoln to evoke shared history. Beware: overuse or misuse can 'burst' the symbol if reality contradicts it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select non-contentious opening subjects to build coalition
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an opening topic which will not only ignore past schisms but will avoid explosive conflicts (e.g., Hughes choosing the spoils system as his opening subject to placate factions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start communications on issues that unite rather than divide the target coalition; use these to create goodwill before approaching harder topics. Anti-pattern: opening with highly polarizing specifics that reawaken old schisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ ambiguous/elastic phrases to mean all things to all men
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'letting the words mean all things to all men' a speaker can repress divisive issues and let a phrase be read differently by different factions (e.g., 'American rights' covering contrasting grievances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use carefully chosen ambiguous language to form coalitions among groups with divergent specific aims. Trade-off: ambiguity can unify short-term support but produces obscurantism and may hide cross-purposes; be wary at crucial points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify complex facts into names/symbols but guard against verbalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers use a shorthand of names and signs to carry complicated situations forward; but if one forgets that one has substituted names for objects, one lapses into verbalism and loses contact with realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symbolic shorthand for cognitive economy, but ensure accuracy by remembering original referents. Anti-pattern: letting names divorced from objects drive policy or messaging decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find common emotional stimuli (transferable emotions) to unite groups
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can find a stimulus that arouses the same emotion in many people (e.g., 'Americanism'), it can be substituted for diverse original stimuli and unite otherwise divided factions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify emotions that are widely shared and link them to a neutral or flexible symbol to form coalitions. Example: 'Americanism' read differently by different voters but binding them together. Measure: effectiveness in producing similar affect across segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit conditioned response and associative stimuli
rubrics_metrics.description: By conditioned response an emotion is not attached merely to one idea but can be attached to ideas of that thing, and then to similar ideas in sequence; thus emotions and responses can be transferred by association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sequences of symbols and messages that condition desired emotional attachments; use repeated associations to broaden triggers. Anti-pattern: assuming an emotion is bound to one factual stimulus only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutralize irreconcilable issues by obliteration or silence
rubrics_metrics.description: "What cannot be compromised must be obliterated... let us pretend that it does not exist." When there is a question that cannot be compromised, it may be suppressed or ignored in public appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppressing or minimizing intractable issues can keep coalitions intact, but risks alienating those for whom the issue is decisive; use cautiously and be prepared for fallout if suppressed facts re-emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture and control symbols to steer public policy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He who captures the symbols by which public feeling is for the moment contained, controls by that much the approaches of public policy.’ Symbols act as strategic junctions for diverse roads of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to define and own the prevailing symbols (labels, slogans, historical figures) relevant to your issue; losing symbol control means losing influence over policy framing. Tactical note: ambitious factions will contest symbol ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mass communications to attempt a common consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fourteen Points were an attempt to exploit the modern machinery of communication (cable, radio, telegraph, daily press) to start the return to a 'common consciousness' throughout the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage available mass media and simultaneous channels to synchronize ideas and names across broad audiences when seeking to create shared meanings. Example: coordinated, repeated messaging across platforms increases chance of crystallizing public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness at crucial points signals cross-purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost always vagueness at a crucial point in public debate is a symptom of cross-purposes; where superficial harmony is the aim and conflict the fact, obscurantism in a public appeal is the usual result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat excessive vagueness as a red flag: it may indicate unresolved contradictory aims. For high-stakes issues, prefer clarified positions or clearly signposted deliberate ambiguities rather than accidental vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must rhetorically 'heal' schisms to form majority coalitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A leader facing a party schism must 'heal it' by invoking shared history, choosing themes that recall common identity, and by staging rhetoric that forgives or represses past divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft narratives and invocations (shared figures, common history) that reconnect fractured groups; scoring: success measured by breadth of coalition and reduction of salient intra-group differences.
